chunks: "The probe input impedance should be as high as possible compared with the impedance of the node I'm measuring, so it doesn't load it.
A good rule of thumb is at least ten times higher than the source impedance, at every frequency that matters.
For a standard 10x passive probe, that's about 10 megaohms in parallel with 10 to 15 picofarads.
A 1x probe or the scope's raw input is 1 megaohm and a bit more capacitance, perhaps 100 picofarads with the cable.
The key is that the capacitor wins at high frequency: at 100 megahertz, 12 picofarads is only 130 ohms, so the probe isn't a high impedance at all any more.
That's why for a node with 1 kilohm source impedance, a 10x probe starts to attenuate and round the signal above roughly 10 megahertz.
So for general measurements I want high resistance and low capacitance, which is what 10x and active probes give.
The exception is a 50 ohm system, like a transmission line or RF measurement.
There the scope's 50 ohm input is correct, because it terminates the line properly and doesn't create a reflection, though it loads any high-impedance node badly.
In practice I pick the probe by comparing its impedance at the signal's highest frequency with the source impedance."
